FrontierFinance uses checklist-style grading: for a given query, an LLM judge checks a system's answer against each rubric and decides whether the criterion is satisfied, yielding a per-query rubric-satisfaction score.
We use macro over micro averaging so that the metric rewards consistent performance across all queries, rather than excelling on a few high-rubric-count queries at the expense of others.
We score each rubric by majority vote across three independent LLM judges: GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.

With FrontierFinance, we benchmark frontier models and systems using three distinct types of harnesses:
Web search harness: a minimal harness pairing each model with its built-in web search tool, providing a baseline for web-search-only performance.
Finance agent v2 harness: an open-source harness connecting the model to six specialized tools: the SEC EDGAR API, a market price data API, web search, HTML parsing, longHTML search, and a calculator
In-house Samaya agent harness: a production-grade harness combining Samaya's custom models, tools, data index, and retrieval engines, optimized for both quality and efficiency.
We re-implemented the agent orchestration with the LangChain library for maximum compatibility with existing models and frameworks.
We introduced tool call limits of 200 tool calls and 300 seconds, ensuring evaluation under a realistic finite budget.
We applied the same limits to the in-house Samaya agent harness for fair comparison.
We select the three default judge models so that they achieve high agreement with a committee of 9 individual judges.
Using three judges from three different model providers also help alleviate bias caused by any single model family.

AI agents are increasingly deployed for professional investment research, yet no benchmark captures the complexity of the full investor workflow.
Screening & Discovery and Sector, Industry & Macro remain the hardest use cases across all systems, where even the best systems reach only 33% and 39%.
Samaya's in-house system leads at 56.0%, ahead of the strongest frontier model (Claude Fable 5, 49.2%) at roughly 2.2× lower cost

As future LLMs are trained on data postdating the query dates, they may answer from parametric knowledge rather than through active retrieval and tool use-the very capabilities the benchmark is designed to test.
Periodic re-annotation with newer query dates is one way to mitigate this issue.
Use cases such as Screening & Discovery are inherently subjective: two analysts might produce different yet equally valid answers.
A system whose answer overlaps with the rubric may outscore one with an equally correct but differently framed response.
